contract.goal: one platform mechanism for a user-submitted file that performs a business action: admission, persistence before parsing, the UPLOADED/VALIDATED/APPLIED lifecycle mapped onto web-core's operation envelope, bounded-memory reading of untrusted xlsx/csv, header-name row addressing, a declared commit policy, and row-reject artifacts
contract.output: new sources/file-action-spring-boot-starter (library tier, parent common, imports ludwig-bom, package ru.ludwigandreas.fileaction); commons-csv added to ludwig-bom; one <module> entry in the root pom; RuleGroup.UPLOADS added to architecture-rules; a reference order-import action in crud-service-example; README.md + README.ru.md for the new module
constraints: no new in-repo dependency may create a reactor cycle; the direction check in design.md is the record
no second status enum restating OperationStatus's six states (RuleGroup.OPERATIONS)
no XSSFWorkbook/HSSFWorkbook/WorkbookFactory anywhere in the new module; xlsx is read via XSSFReader SAX only; SXSSFWorkbook confined to the write package
nothing is materialised: no readAllBytes, Files.readAllLines, MultipartFile.getBytes, IOUtils.toByteArray
QueryDSL only; the change introduces NO new SQL carve-out
commit-policy has no default and an action omitting it must fail startup
scanning.mode defaults to required and must fail startup with no FileScanner bean
IdempotencyFilter must not be applied to the submit endpoints; the claim goes through IdempotencyStore directly
audit goes through audit-core's single AuditSink; no module-local audit SPI, no second redaction mask, no try/catch around record
no hard-coded user-facing text; i18n bundle key sets identical across both locales
every new convention gets a mechanical check or a comment at the point of the rule saying why none is possible
no shared operation table; web-core gains no persistence dependency
done_when: scripts/manifest.sh build && scripts/manifest.sh stale && scripts/manifest.sh layout

decisions: done_when adds scripts/check_image_pins.sh and scripts/check_api_baseline.sh, which scripts/gate.sh --list prints but tasks.md group 9 omitted. The contract is authoritative; tasks.md group 9 is to be corrected to match rather than the reverse.

A ludwig-bom change plus a root-pom module addition means the gate is the whole reactor (mvn clean install), as gate.sh states for a bom or parent module. No narrower gate is acceptable for this change.

Task 1.1 named `help:effective-pom | grep ludwig-bom` as proof the BOM import works; that is wrong, because an import-scope BOM is resolved away in the effective POM. The real evidence is `mvn -pl :file-action-spring-boot-starter dependency:tree` showing commons-csv 1.12.0 and poi 5.4.1 resolving with no version declared in the module POM, which it does.

RowOutcome needed an explicit Disposition enum (APPLIED/REJECTED/SKIPPED). The first version had rejected() and skipped() returning identical records, so the documented distinction - SKIPPED must not count toward reject-threshold, or a file of intentional duplicates fails as 'the wrong file' - did not exist in the data.

A literal no-break space in ColumnBinding tripped Checkstyle's NonAsciiSourceText. Resolved the way export's CsvProfile resolves the byte-order mark: a private static final char built from the code point, with a comment saying why it is not a character literal. Any future invisible character in this module takes the same form.

FileActionState keeps REJECTED and EXPIRED even though both are words in OperationVocabularyRules' shared sets. Verified against the rule's implementation: it fires only when EVERY constant is a shared word, and UPLOADED/VALIDATED/APPLYING/APPLIED are not, so the enum is a richer lifecycle rather than a restatement - exactly the RemoteJobState case the rule's javadoc blesses. The first version of FileActionStateMappingTest asserted no name overlap at all, which was stricter than the rule it claimed to describe; it now asserts the rule's actual discriminator.

RowReaderFactory.open takes a local Path, not an InputStream. POI's OPCPackage.open(InputStream) reads the whole package into the heap; only the File overload reads lazily from the ZIP central directory, which is also what makes ArchiveInspector's metadata-only bomb check possible. A spooled temp file is bounded by the action's size ceiling and is not the materialisation the module forbids - that is holding the file in the heap. Recorded in RowReaderFactory's javadoc.

RowReader hands rows to a RowVisitor instead of returning an Iterator. The XLSX reader is a SAX parse, which is push-based; converting push to pull needs a producer thread and a bounded queue or a buffer of rows, and neither is justified. The CSV reader follows the same shape so the engine has one path.

ArchiveInspector enforces the per-action ZIP ceilings itself rather than relying on POI's ZipSecureFile, because POI's knob is a JVM-global static and so cannot be a per-action ceiling - export shares the JVM and reads admin-supplied templates under different assumptions. POI's global stays as a conservative backstop for sizes the central directory lies about. Both mechanisms are documented at ArchiveInspector so neither is removed as redundant.

CellCoercion returns a Coerced record, not Optional<Object>. An Optional cannot hold null, so 'blank cell, record accepts null' and 'not coercible at all' both arrived as Optional.empty() - which would have rejected every row with a blank optional cell. Caught by RowCoercionTest.handlesEmptyCells.

Localised date patterns are also tried with the year widened from yy to yyyy. en-US's FormatStyle.SHORT is M/d/yy and MEDIUM is MMM d, y, so between them the two localised styles reject '2/1/2026' - the commonest way an American caller types a date. Caught by RowCoercionTest.parsesADateInTheCallersLocale.

claimForProcessing is a select-then-update pair through the ORM rather than job-core's SkipLockedClaim UPDATE ... RETURNING. The submission row carries a @Version and a concurrent cancel writes it; going round the ORM would bypass optimistic locking and lose the cancel. A row another instance claims in between fails the update's state predicate rather than being claimed twice. Recorded at the method.

Task 4.1's Liquibase integration test and task 6.1's confinement tests were written out of order (6.1 first), because the confinement rules had to exist before more production code was written against the reader, not after. Both are complete.

PoiConfinementTest and NoMaterialisationTest were verified red by temporarily adding a class calling new XSSFWorkbook(in) and Files.readAllBytes: 3 of 7 assertions failed, naming both rules. The probe class was deleted and the suite is green at 125 tests. The repo's own standard - an architecture test never seen red is one nobody should trust - is why this was done rather than assumed.

The bound rows are always written to a local newline-delimited JSON artifact during the read, and the apply streams them back. Three things fall out of one decision: a CONFIRM-mode action applies what it showed the user rather than re-binding the workbook against reference data that may have changed; a DocumentHandler gets a genuinely lazy Stream with no thread and no buffer, which a push-based SAX reader cannot give it; and DIRECT and CONFIRM become one apply path instead of two, only one of which the cautious mode would exercise.

ApplyPass uses a programmatic TransactionTemplate rather than @Transactional, because the transaction boundary is precisely what varies per action and an annotation's boundary is fixed at compile time. ALL_OR_NOTHING therefore reads the artifact inside its single transaction and holds a connection for the whole traversal - unavoidable, since that is what the policy promises - which is why a large file on that policy belongs on a DEFERRED action. Stated at the method.

RecordingTransactionManager asserts commit-versus-rollback, not just the applied count. PER_BATCH and PER_ROW share a transaction boundary and differ only in what a rejected row does to it, so a test counting applied rows alone passes for both on a clean file and would not notice the two being swapped.

The deferred worker deliberately does NOT hold a RunLock, while the retention job does. Instances processing different submissions concurrently is the point of the worker and claimForProcessing keeps two off the same one; a cluster-wide lock there would make a whole deployment's throughput that of one pod. Retention has no per-item parallelism to gain and several instances deleting the same objects is pure waste, so one holder at a time is correct. Both reasons are recorded at the classes.

Retention deletes the objects before marking the row EXPIRED. The other order would leave a row claiming its artifacts are gone while they are still in the bucket - a leak nothing notices; this order can at worst orphan an object, which is visible in a bucket listing and is logged.

The deferred worker's lease, batch size, attempt cap, interval and drain timeout are configuration under ludwig.file-action.deferred rather than constants. They were literals first and Checkstyle's MagicNumber flagged them, which was the right prompt: every one of them is a value a deployment may need to tune against its own file sizes.

UploadRules names MultipartFile as a string rather than compiling against spring-web, for the reason architecture-rules hand-rolls its JSON report writer: a rules library that compiled against every framework it has an opinion about would make every consuming service inherit all of them. spring-web is added at test scope only, so the bad.uploads fixture can name the type. The rule's three deliberate blind spots - reactive uploads, a raw byte[] body, and how the sanctioned module itself behaves - are listed in its javadoc.

Enabling the shared rule groups (task 6.2) reported 11 failures and 8 of them were real defects, now fixed rather than disabled: a config -> web -> engine -> config package cycle, a JPA entity reaching the controller, a repository injected into the controller, an IOException caught in the web package, an unversioned base path, Optional as a field and parameter type in two classes, and configuration properties with no constraints. The task was worth doing for the findings rather than the passes.

The engine takes a FileActionSettings record rather than FileActionProperties. That closed the package cycle and is better regardless: a Spring properties tree is a binding artefact with nullable override fields, and an engine that reads one cannot be constructed in a test without building it.

FileActionService returns SubmissionSnapshot and RejectView, never an entity. A detached JPA entity in a controller is a LazyInitializationException waiting for somebody to add a field, which presents as a 500 on a request that previously worked.

The controller's base path is a fixed constant, not a property. rest-paths reads the literal annotation value, so a value containing a ${...} placeholder can never match a path pattern - the rule was unsatisfiable, not merely unsatisfied - and it was pointing at something real: a starter whose endpoints move per deployment is one no client can be written against.

FileActionService.submit takes a ContentSource (a supplier that may throw) rather than an InputStream, so the controller passes file::getInputStream and catches nothing. exceptions.controllers-do-not-catch-checked-exceptions covers the whole web package, so an earlier attempt that moved the catch into a web-package helper class did not satisfy it - correctly.

UploadSpool throws the module's own FileRejectedException rather than a private UploadTooLargeException converted at the boundary. The message, the status and the code all belong to the ceiling rather than to the spool, and the second exception class was one more thing outside web-core's single ProblemDetail pipeline for no gain.

Three rules stay disabled with reasons at the point of the disable: layering and repositories-are-used-only-by-services and transactional-methods-are-in-the-service-layer (this module has no service package in the shape the rules describe), controllers-do-not-call-controllers (34 violations, all the same private-helper call inside one controller; object-storage disables it for the same reason), and custom-exceptions-extend-the-base-exception (SheetHandler.StopParsing is a SAX early-exit signal with a suppressed stack trace that must never reach the ProblemDetail pipeline).

ludwig.file-action.defaults.max-rows is 5000, matching the inline ceiling, because execution defaults to INLINE. It was 100000 against an inline ceiling of 5000, which meant every action failed startup out of the box - a starter whose own defaults contradict each other is not configurable, it is broken. A new defaults.max-rows-limit (100000) is the module's absolute declared ceiling, and the refusal above it names file-ingest-spring-boot-starter.

LargeWorkbookHeapIT asserts a ratio - how much more the large read retains than a small one - rather than an absolute byte ceiling. A fixed number would be tuned to whichever machine first ran it and would go red on a CI agent with a different collector, which is how a test like this ends up disabled. It carries a fourth case that performs a DOM read of the same file and asserts it retains at least five times more, so the measurement is proven capable of failing rather than assumed to be.

The heap guarantee is split in two. LargeWorkbookHeapIT keeps the deterministic half - every row of a hundred thousand is read, the last one is intact - and runs on every build. LargeWorkbookHeapMeasurementIT holds the ratio measurement behind @Tag("measurement"), excluded by the overridable property file-action.test.excluded.groups, exactly as export excludes its load test and for the same recorded reason: a heap ratio measured in a JVM shared with other test classes and instrumented by JaCoCo passed alone and failed in the full suite, and a flaky guarantee is worse than an honest tag.

claimForProcessing is @Transactional(REQUIRES_NEW) - its own transaction, not the caller's. The claim must be visible to other instances before the work starts; a claim sharing the apply's transaction would only become visible when the apply committed, by which time a second instance has claimed the same submission.

The reference product-import action adds no Liquibase changeset, contrary to what task 8.1 anticipated. It writes through ProductService into catalog_product, which already exists - an import is a different way in to an action the service already performs, not a second implementation with a table of its own. Inventing a table to satisfy the task's wording would have been worse, so the task is complete with that part deliberately not done and the reason recorded at the handler and in the service's master changelog.

The authority is checked on the reads as well as the writes. A submission's envelope carries its filename, row counts and failure reason, and the rejects resource carries the contents of the user's own cells, so 'who may poll this' is the same question as 'who may submit it'. There is deliberately no permissive fallback when security is absent: that would turn a configured authority into one that silently is not checked, so the startup validator refuses that combination instead. The checker accepts the authority with or without Spring Security's ROLE_ prefix, which is the mistake every deployment makes once.

A CONFIRM-mode submit answers 202, not 200, because a VALIDATED submission is not terminal and the operation contract requires a 200 from a submit endpoint to carry a terminal envelope. The confirm then answers 200. The reference integration test asserts both, because the first version asserted 200 on the submit and was wrong about the contract rather than about the code.
failures: addLocalised called getLocalizedDateTimePattern(null, null, ...) on the date-only path, which throws, and the method's own catch swallowed it - so no localised date pattern was ever added and only the ISO fallback worked. Fixed by passing the style as dateStyle always; the comment at the point of the fix records it. Caught by RowCoercionTest, not by review.

AnnotatedReportWriter first placed the problems column one past the widest row seen so far, which moved the column part-way down a ragged sheet and made the report unreadable in a spreadsheet. Fixed to a column derived from the header row, with the trade-off (a value beyond the last header column is overwritten, and was never read by the import either) stated at the field. AnnotatedReportWriterTest.theProblemsColumnIsFixed is the regression test.

NoSqlStringsTest's first regex used [^"]* either side of the keyword, which spans newlines, so it matched the ordinary code and comments BETWEEN two unrelated string literals and failed on an entity's column declarations. Bounded to [^"\n]* with the reason recorded at the pattern: a rule that cries wolf is a rule that gets deleted.

The bound-row artifact first stored the payload alone, so a handler-originated reject had no row address - and because RejectCollector ignores a reject with no problems, it was silently not counted either. A handler saying 'unknown SKU' with no row number is useless to the user, which is the point of the module. Fixed by introducing BoundRow<R>, which carries sheet and displayed row alongside the payload; the handler still sees only its own row type. Caught by CommitPolicyTest.perRowAppliesTheRest, which now asserts the reject names row 15 of sheet Orders.

Tasks 5.1 and 5.2 were ticked on the production code existing, before FileActionControllerTest, ProblemMapperTest and NoLocalAdviceTest had been written or run. That is not what the task's named verification means, and the apply guidance is explicit about it. Un-ticked and the tests written. 5.5 was ticked with FileActionAutoConfigurationTest also missing; it is listed here for the same reason and corrected in the same pass.

The shipped defaults contradicted each other: defaults.max-rows 100000, inline.max-rows 5000, execution INLINE, so FileActionConfigurationValidator refused any action a deployment had not already overridden. Found by FileActionAutoConfigurationTest refusing to start a context with one ordinary action in it - which is exactly the out-of-the-box experience the module claims to provide, and the only test that would have caught it.

FileActionPersistenceAutoConfiguration omitted repositoryBaseClass = BaseRepositoryImpl.class, so Spring Data tried to derive a query from db-core's getByIdOrThrow and every consuming context failed at startup with 'No property throw found'. idempotency's copy of the same class documents this exact failure; found by FileActionSchemaIT, which was the first context to start the repositories at all.

The module injected TaskScheduler by type. A consuming service with idempotency and outbox on its classpath has three, so startup failed with 'expected single matching bean but found 3' - the normal case for a real service, not an edge one. Fixed by owning a named fileActionTaskScheduler and injecting it with @Qualifier, which is what every scheduled starter here does.

FileActionService used getReferenceById outside any transaction and then read fields off the returned proxy, so every integration test failed with LazyInitializationException. Replaced with a reload(id) that does a real findById. The proxy is correct inside SubmissionStore, where a transaction is open, and wrong everywhere else - which is the same hazard SubmissionSnapshot exists to document.

claimForProcessing ran a QueryDSL update with no transaction, so the deferred worker's first tick in production would have failed with 'Executing an update/delete query' and no submission would ever have been processed. Found by DeferredClaimIT.

Rejects were persisted and the error report published BEFORE the apply, so a handler-originated reject was counted but never stored: a caller saw 'rowsRejected: 1' with an empty rejects resource and nothing in the downloadable report. Reordered so both happen after the apply, with an addRejects variant for the confirm path that must not delete the cell-level rejects the user was shown. Found by DeferredClaimIT.theRejectIsAddressed.

required-authority was configured, validated at startup, documented in both READMEs and named in the capability spec - and never actually checked. Nothing in the service or the controller read it. That is the worst shape a security control can take, because every artefact around it says it is present. Found while wiring the reference action in crud-service-example, by noticing the authority name I had invented was granted to nobody and wondering why no test failed. Fixed with an AuthorityChecker seam, a FileActionForbiddenException (403), enforcement on all six entry points including the reads, and AuthorityEnforcementTest with ten cases - one of which asserts nothing is stored when the caller is refused, so the check is provably before the work.

The changelog declared content_sha256 as char(64). Postgres implements char(n) as bpchar, which Hibernate's schema validation reports as a type mismatch against the entity's String - so any consuming service with ddl-auto=validate refused to start. Changed to varchar(64), with the reason at the column. The module's own ITs could not catch it because they do not validate the schema against the entities; crud-service-example does.

The module published an unqualified Clock bean guarded by @ConditionalOnMissingBean. rest-client-spring-boot-starter publishes ludwigRestClientClock, so a service with both had two Clock beans and cache-spring-boot-starter's registry - which injects one by type - failed to start on an ambiguity neither module caused alone. This is the exact trap idempotency and audit already document for JPAQueryFactory. Fixed by resolving a clock through ObjectProvider.getIfUnique() with a systemUTC fallback and publishing no bean at all.

The new module was absent from build/jacoco-aggregate/pom.xml, so its 11507 instructions were missing from the platform coverage number and the build stayed green either way. Caught by scripts/check_aggregate_report.py, which exists for exactly that - and which the change's own gate step 9.6 called for. Added; the report now covers 28 of 28 jar modules and the module sits at 84.0%.

Removing the module's Clock bean broke its own integration tests, which autowired one. The right fix was in the tests, not the module: an application that wants a Clock declares it, which is what a real deployment does. Found by the full reactor build, not by the module's own verify, because the module had been installed before the bean was removed.
